transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-25
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: ~63 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Alex Chen (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Infra), Tom Walker (ML Eng), James O'Neal (Security), Lina Gomez (Platform), Robert Yao (Procurement)

Summary (auto):
Short technical deep dive for on-prem / air-gapped deployment. Covered artifact delivery, offline licensing, GPU driver matrix, performance tuning (batching, KV cache, quantization), and validation plan. Action items assigned for offline bundle, driver matrix, and sample workload.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a 60 minute deep dive — Alex is gonna drive the tech bits — brief intros?
[00:08] Priya: Hi I'm Priya infra lead at AcmeBank. We run most things in our datacenter, a couple of clusters on prem with strict egress rules, airgapped in some zones.
[00:15] Tom: Tom, ML eng, I'll be running the benchmarks and model validation.
[00:20] James: James from security, here for compliance questions.
[00:23] Lina: Lina platform, ops.
[00:25] Robert: Robert procurement, quick questions about licensing later.
[00:28] Maya: Great. Alex?
[00:30] Alex: Thanks. So agenda: offline artifact delivery, install flow for air-gapped, license entitlements and offline activation, supported GPU/driver matrix, and then runtime performance topics — batching, KV cache, quantization, latency/throughput tradeoffs — and finally validation plan.
[00:48] Alex: Quick note, I'll mention some product names — sometimes transcripts flip names — our dedicated runtime is called Redwood Dedicated and the private offering is Redwood Private, you may hear me say "Redwood Dedi" or, uh, "Redwood Private control plane" interchangeably.
[01:00] Priya: Good. Primary ask from infra: we need a signed artifact bundle we can pull into our isolated repo, and an installation runbook that doesn't require internet access.
[01:08] Alex: Absolutely. We provide a tarball signed with our corporate GPG and also an entitlement/license file. For airgapped installs we include an install script, systemd units, the runtime docker image tarball (for preloaded registries), and a validation harness with perf scripts.
[01:22] Tom: What's in the runtime image — is it full docker images or OCI blobs? Any external dependencies like apt pulls?
[01:28] Alex: It's full docker images exported as tarballs and an image registry bundle you can import. The install script is intentionally offline-first — it will not attempt apt or curl by default. We do include an optional helper that can ship in a separate bundle for pulling updates if you allow a transient egress window.
[01:46] James: On the security side we need signed hashes, an SBOM, and a signed entitlement that maps to our license. Also audit hooks.
[01:53] Maya: Yep, we'll deliver SBOM, SHA256 checksums for every artifact and a PGP/GPG signature for the bundle. For audit hooks we can provide the offline logging agent that writes event logs locally; if you require central logging we can discuss a secure relay but that's a separate convo.
[02:11] Priya: Driver versions — we've had lots of trouble with mismatched CUDA/cuDNN combos. What matrix do you support?
[02:19] Alex: Good question. Our recommended baseline is NVIDIA driver 525+ with CUDA 11.8 for a wide set of models, but for newer kernels and better kernel selection we recommend NVIDIA 535+ and CUDA 12.1 for H100 and the latest A100 optimizations. We'll send a full driver matrix (we have it as a spreadsheet) showing recommended driver/CUDA/cuDNN/cuBLAS combos per GPU and per model family.
[02:40] Tom: Does the runtime require a specific NCCL version for multi-GPU NVLink?
[02:44] Alex: Yes, NCCL 2.14+ recommended for A100/H100 setups; if you're doing tensor-parallel or sharded KV cache we prefer NCCL 2.15. We'll include the NCCL libs inside the bundle to avoid needing system installs, but the kernel module and driver must match the GPU driver.
[03:02] Priya: How about GPUs — will your runtime do well on both A100 and H100? We have both in our lab.
[03:08] Alex: Yes, we support both. For H100 we get better fp16 throughput and some proprietary kernels; on A100 we have tuned kernels that are performant. Quantization profiles differ — for int8 quant we have model-specific profiles; we'll share recommended quantization profiles for the models you'll run.
[03:23] Lina: Can you explain the quantization support — we want to know the tradeoffs for 8-bit vs 16-bit and how you validate accuracy regressions.
[03:31] Alex: Sure — we support per-channel symmetric int8 for many transformer weights (LLM.int8-type workflows) and also 4-bit experimental profiles. The runtime can run in int8 lowering mode where activations still use fp16 for attention softmax stability. We ship evaluation harnesses with a reference prompt set so you can run regression tests — accuracy deltas are measured and we flag model-specific thresholds. We recommend starting with int8 for cost-sensitive workloads but roll forward only after running the eval suite.
[03:59] Tom: Does quantization impact KV cache behavior?
[04:02] Alex: Slightly. KV cache stores keys/values in the format the runtime uses — when using int8 weights with fp16 activations the KV cache remains fp16 in most configs to avoid p99 jitter. We do have a compact KV mode which compresses KVs on disk using 16-bit or half-precision representations to save memory, but we usually keep in-GPU KVs as fp16 for latency-sensitive apps.
[04:26] Priya: Latency targets — we need p99 < 250ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) in our interactive UI. Is that realistic?
[04:33] Alex: Depends on model size and batch policy — for a 7B model on a single A100 with optimized kernel and small-batching we often hit p50 ~60-80ms and p99 ~160-220ms for 128-token streams. For 70B or 100B models you'll need multi-gpu or sequence parallelism; p99 will increase. The KV warmup is important — cold-cache first request will be higher.
[04:58] Tom: What's the best batching strategy for interactive SLOs?
[05:02] Alex: For interactive you want small window batching — e.g., 20-40ms collection window or use adaptive batching where you cap batch size to maintain a p99 target. Redwood runtime supports latency-aware batching where requests are prioritized and a batch flush policy based on either time or max tokens. We can share config examples: batch_window_ms, max_tokens_per_batch, and per-route overrides.
[05:23] Priya: Can we control batching per route? We have both chat UI and async embedding jobs.
[05:27] Alex: Yes, routing policies let you set per-route batching, pref max_latency_ms and throughput targets. Embeddings get very high throughput batching; chat routes get tighter latency caps.
[05:36] James: Telemetry in airgapped — what do you collect and can it be disabled?
[05:40] Alex: By default we collect anonymized runtime metrics and traces to our hosted backend, but for air-gapped installs we offer a telemetry-off mode. We provide a local metrics agent that stores metrics in a local time-series and can export to your offline SIEM. If you want, we have a secure relay agent that can be run in a DMZ to push only hashes and usage pings — all opt-in.
[06:00] Lina: If telemetry is off, do we lose auto kernel selection / adaptive batching intelligence?
[06:05] Alex: No, the runtime's adaptive heuristics run locally. The cloud-only pieces are for global analytics and suggested config optimizations. You still get local kernel selection based on hardware probes during startup.
[06:17] Tom: Performance testing — what harness do you provide?
[06:20] Alex: We include a load-gen harness: a python runner that can replay prompts with configurable token distribution, concurrency, and client-side latencies. It also has a perf collector that emits p50/p90/p99, throughput (tokens/sec), and GPU utilization traces (nvidia-smi sampling). For airgapped we'll include prebuilt binaries for the perf collector.
[06:41] Priya: About GPU firmware and driver updates — we tend to be conservative. If we can't upgrade drivers easily can you support older drivers?
[06:48] Alex: We certify a range — we'll provide a supported matrix and a compatibility badge. Older drivers may work but you might miss kernel-level optimizations; we'll flag known regressions. In critical cases we can provide backported kernel patches inside the runtime, but that has to be vetted with your security team.
[07:07] James: Offline licensing — what's the model?
[07:10] Maya: We issue an entitlement file that binds to a hardware fingerprint (machine serials or cluster UUID) and has a signed expiration. For airgapped installs the SE will generate the license file based on the asset IDs you provide and we sign it. Activation is offline — you drop the file into /etc/redwood/license and runtime validates the signature.
[07:29] Robert: Any offline license generator? We prefer not to send hardware IDs externally.
[07:33] Alex: We can accept a signed CSR from your side and do a double-signed entitlement, or you can provide hardware fingerprints hashed locally. We have a flow where you share an encrypted blob and we produce a license without storing raw IDs. We'll document the flow.
[07:48] Tom: Model variants and fallback — if Dedicated capacity is full can the runtime fallback to a smaller quantized variant automatically?
[07:55] Alex: In hosted mode we do routing fallbacks; in private deployment you can configure automatic model fallbacks on the control plane side if you run our optional control plane; for fully offline installs the policy runs locally — we provide a compatible model bundle with smaller variants and a policy to prefer fallback in low-memory conditions.
[08:14] Priya: Where do we store model artifacts locally? NFS or local SSD? We have both and worry about latency with NFS.
[08:21] Alex: We recommend local NVMe for active model shards and use NFS for cold storage. The runtime has a model cache manager that prefetches shards to local NVMe based on hotset heuristics. For multi-node setups we recommend a shared pre-warm step to prime local SSDs.
[08:37] Tom: KV cache sharing across replicas — if we have multiple replicas behind a LB can they share KV cache?
[08:43] Alex: Not directly. KV cache is per-process GPU-local for latency reasons. We have a prefix cache that can be exported and imported between instances to warm others, but live shared KV across GPUs is typically not supported because of synchronous latency constraints. You can use a prewarm service that ships prefixes to new replicas.
[09:03] Priya: What about disk encryption and KMS integration — we need HSM compatibility.
[09:09] Alex: We support customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest. For air-gapped installs we can integrate with your on-prem HSM via PKCS#11 for key ops. The license and artifact signing can be validated against your HSM-based root.
[09:25] James: Audit logs — what format and retention?
[09:29] Alex: We write standard JSON lines with timestamps and event types (inference.request, model.load, license.verify). You can point logs to local syslog. Retention is configurable; for demo bundles we set 90 days by default but we'll tune to your policy.
[09:45] Tom: A few deep runtime Qs — how do you handle KV cache eviction and memory compaction?
[09:50] Alex: We use LRU-ish policies for prefix caching, and a periodic compaction step that runs when GPU memory pressure crosses thresholds. Compaction is careful to avoid introducing jitter — it's throttled to background epochs. You can configure eviction aggressiveness and warm-up windows.
[10:09] Tom: Batching internals — say we have mixed short and long requests, how are tokens packed?
[10:14] Alex: We do length-aware packing: group similar-length requests and pad to a bucket. Also we do per-token budget caps to avoid a single long request monopolizing a batch. The runtime supports token-aware prioritization and stream-flushing to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[10:30] Priya: Are there diagnostics for kernel stalls or CUDA errors?
[10:34] Alex: Yes we ship a diagnostics tool that captures CUDA errors, kernel latency histograms, and stack traces for the runtime threads. For airgapped we'll include verbose logging builds if you want them.
[10:45] Lina: For acceptance testing, what's the recommended runbook?
[10:49] Alex: Recommended runbook: 1) import images and verify checksums, 2) install drivers and validate GPU using NVIDIA's smi and deviceQuery, 3) import model bundles to local storage, 4) run smoke tests (model load + small inference), 5) run perf suite (cold->warm prefixes, mixed workload), 6) run regression eval suite. We'll hand you a checklist and sample scripts.
[11:10] Priya: Can we get a signed attestation that the bundles are unchanged after download?
[11:14] Maya: Yes, GPG signature plus signed manifest; we can also provide a notarized hash via a third-party if needed.
[11:22] Robert: Pricing and how offline licensing affects commercial terms?
[11:26] Maya: Offline licensing is the same seat/throughput-based model; there is an enterprise fee for airgapped support which covers artifact delivery and special SLAs. I'll follow up with commercial details after this call.
[11:36] Tom: Any caveats running on ARM nodes?
[11:39] Alex: We have limited support for ARM64 GPUs; most of our production kernels are x86_64 optimized. For ARM we can provide builds but some kernels might be not as tuned. We'll flag that in the driver matrix.
[11:52] Priya: About model updates — how do we securely apply patches?
[11:55] Alex: Offline update flow: we deliver incremental bundles with signed deltas. You validate signatures, import, and then the runtime can perform an atomic swap of model shards to avoid in-flight errors. We document rollback steps.
[12:13] James: If we find backend telemetry disabled, will Redwood be able to help debug issues?
[12:17] Alex: Yes — we provide a debug bundle you can run that produces detailed traces which you can share with us over a secure channel (SFTP or encrypted USB). There's also a vendor-on-site option if needed.
[12:30] Priya: We should schedule the validation window.
[12:32] Maya: Agreed — propose 2 day window starting 2025-04-14, team to confirm.
[12:36] Robert: Procurement will need the license terms and SOW.
[12:38] Maya: I'll send SOW and license template.
[12:40] Alex: Quick note on perf numbers — for your sample 7B chat model we can target ~2000 tok/sec on A100 and ~3500 on H100 under batched inference with batch sizes ~8-16, depending on prompt distribution.
[12:56] Tom: Can we get sample logs showing nvprof/gpu utilization from similar customers?
[12:59] Alex: We'll scrub PII and send anonymized traces from an internal lab and a reference customer.
[13:07] Priya: Any gotchas for SELinux / locked-down kernels?
[13:10] Alex: SELinux can block the runtime's mmap patterns; we'll include an SELinux policy you can apply. There are also seccomp profiles.
[13:21] Maya: ok going to recap next steps — Alex will prepare the offline artifact bundle + checksums and driver matrix; Maya will send license template, SOW, and pricing; Priya/Tom will confirm GPU driver baseline and sample workload; schedule validation 2025-04-14 tentative.
[13:37] Lina: Thanks all — we'll coordinate internally.
[13:40] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with artifacts and a calendar invite.

End of transcript.
